At the end of the entire training episode, the trained models for each agent is saved, and can be deployed for use in the testing phase. Table 3 reveals the hyper-parameters used during the training of each DRL agent.
Although actor–critic algorithms such as SAC, A3C and PPO are popular for continuous control, we deliberately adopt a value based Deep Q Network (DQN) for the proposed EMS because it matches the structure and computational constraints of our problem. The agents do not output generic continuous controls, but select one multiplier from a finite catalogue of discrete error factors that scale the forecast error standard deviation of each stochastic parameter, which yields a large yet finite combinatorial action space that is naturally handled by DQN, whereas a continuous policy would still need to be projected back to the nearest admissible multiplier, breaking the assumptions of policy gradient updates and introducing additional approximation errors. Moreover, every environment step requires solving the single level MPEC with the transformed stochastic parameters to compute the feasibility penalties
R _ { 2 } ,
so off-policy data reuse is crucial; on-policy methods such as SAC, A3C and PPO would demand many more fresh trajectories and therefore many more expensive MPEC solves, while DQN uses a replay buffer that allows extensive reuse of past transitions. In addition, the reward landscape induced by deviation and penalty terms can be highly non smooth, so policy gradient methods may suffer from noisy and unstable gradients unless heavily regularized, whereas value based DQN learns Q values from temporal difference targets without differentiating through the environment, which typically yields lower variance targets and makes training less sensitive to hyperparameters such as learning rate and entropy regularization. Finally, DQN provides simple and transparent exploration control through an epsilon greedy policy, which is easy to tune in the presence of large negative rewards for infeasible or highly suboptimal schedules, while entropy regularization in SAC or PPO can encourage overly aggressive exploration in regions that consistently produce infeasible operating points, which is undesirable given the high cost of each environment evaluation.
4.2 . Testing process
The testing phase is as described in Fig. 4. Here, given the day-ahead predictions of the stochastic parameters (load, solar, and wind) from the ERs and MGs, the hourly mean and standard deviation from the historical data (2007–2009), these inputs are fed into the commensurately trained agent(s).
The agent(s) then perform the transformations internally, and sends these transformed values as inputs to the deterministic bi-level NMG framework from where the optimal schedules and objectives are derived. The testing process all happens on a timescale of milli-seconds when compared with the time required for uncertainty handling with the stochastic optimization methods showcased as benchmarks in this work. It is critical to note here that a larger network does not necessarily translate to a proportionate increase in the number of DRL agents in the L-MADRL framework. While it is true that ERs and MG operators are modelled by different agents, each agent is designed to handle multiple nodes that share the same type of stochastic parameter (for example, wind at ERs, wind at MGs, solar at
\mathbf { M G s } ,
or load at MGs). In other words, the number of agents scales with the number of distinct uncertainty types, not with the number of buses. Hence, when the system size increases, what grows is primarily the action space of some agents, not the agent count itself. Alternatively, for scalability and faster learning, the action space because of the larger network could be partitioned across two or more agents that each cover a subset of nodes. This was precisely what was done for agents 4 and 5 in the 14-bus case which handled the load demand uncertainty, since nine (9) buses had load attached, they were split between two agents; agent 4 handled five of the nine load buses and agent 5 handled the remaining four. Either way, both design choices remain compatible with our L-MADRL framework.
5 . Two-stage stochastic optimization
This section describes the procedures involved in implementing the two-stage risk-neutral and the risk-averse stochastic optimization with CVaR. The uncertainty modeling technique used is described first alongside the scenario generation/reduction process.
5.1 . Uncertainty modelling
Accurately modeling the uncertainties of stochastic parameters by considering only deterministic forecasts is too risky, and could lead to sub-optimal schedules especially when planning to participate in a dayahead or real-time electricity market. To circumvent this, MCS could be utilized in generating multiple plausible scenarios of these variable parameters in the next hour, or next day as the case may be. This process is the ’scenario generation’ phase and it relies on using accurate PDFs that closely fits the stochastic parameters. In this work, the normal distribution was used to model the stochasticity of the load demand, while the beta and weibull distributions were used to model that of the solar irradiance and wind speed respectively.
